executive_summary.headline: addyosmani/agent-skills (47.5k stars) and mattpocock/skills (112k stars) land the week's clearest message: agent skills are now a software engineering discipline with specs, quality gates, versioning, and test suites — not a prompt file you paste into a README
executive_summary.body: Two senior-engineer skill libraries dominated the week's GitHub signal. Addy Osmani's agent-skills (47.5k stars) packages a seven-command development lifecycle — /spec, /plan, /build, /test, /review, /code-simplify, /ship — grounded in Google engineering practices, including Hyrum's Law, the Beyonce Rule, trunk-based development, and the test pyramid. Matt Pocock's skills (112k stars) surfaces the same idea from an independent practitioner angle: 18 skills structured around real failure modes in Claude Code and Codex, with the /request-refactor-plan skill showing 3.20x agent success improvement on evals. Both repos install in one command and work across Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

executive_summary.headline: NVIDIA/SkillSpector ships the first dedicated pre-installation security scanner for agent skills — 64 vulnerability patterns across 16 categories including MCP tool poisoning, supply-chain CVE lookups via OSV.dev, and taint tracking — Apache-2.0, 5.3k stars
executive_summary.body: SkillSpector addresses the supply-chain risk introduced by the now-large agent skills ecosystem. It scans git repos, URLs, zip files, or directories before installation, running fast static analysis then optionally an LLM semantic pass. It checks for prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, excessive agency, memory poisoning, MCP tool poisoning (TP1–TP4), and YARA-matched malware signatures. NVIDIA's own claim: over 26% of common agent skills contain vulnerabilities. Output is terminal, JSON, Markdown, or SARIF; a 0–100 risk score with severity labels. The tool is directly paired with the addyosmani/agent-skills wave — the same week that skills frameworks grew significantly, a dedicated scanner appeared.

executive_summary.headline: commensa-ai/commensa-audit (Show HN, June 10) measured the hidden cost of AI-generated PRs: 27% of agent-built code in a 162-PR sprint was the AI correcting its own earlier work — the first production-scale rework audit released as an open-source tool
executive_summary.body: commensa-audit reads git history and classifies every PR by signal cascade: explicit corrective reverts → self-correction (predominantly undoing lines added in the prior N days) → churn-cluster membership → otherwise generative. On commensa-ai's own 162-PR, 13-day sprint, 27% of PRs were AI self-correction. The tool produces an HTML report, JSON export, and per-PR CSV. This is not a theoretical concern: 27% rework tax on a 162-PR dataset is a concrete cost of agentic development that is now quantifiable and trackable.

executive_summary.headline: Key takeaway: The week of June 8–14 converged on skills governance — three independent signals (addyosmani/agent-skills, mattpocock/skills, NVIDIA/SkillSpector) established that agent skills need the same version control, test suites, and security scanning as code dependencies. The rework audit from commensa-ai completed the picture: production agent pipelines that lack quality gates pay a measurable 27% correction tax.
executive_summary.body: The week's pattern is consistent: as agentic coding moves from prototype to production-speed workflows (sermakarevich/fleet demonstrated 3 parallel agents running continuously, hitting Claude's $200 subscription limit in 30 minutes), the engineering discipline around skills — what they do, whether they are safe, whether they produce net-new code — has become the constraint. An enterprise AI team deploying agent skills without SkillSpector pre-scanning and without a quality gate library like addyosmani/agent-skills is accepting supply-chain risk and a potential 27% rework overhead on every sprint.

top_picks.title: NVIDIA/SkillSpector
top_picks.subtitle: Security scanner for AI agent skills — 64 vulnerability patterns, 16 categories, MCP tool poisoning detection, live OSV.dev CVE lookups, Apache-2.0, 5.3k stars
top_picks.author: NVIDIA
top_picks.summary: SkillSpector scans AI agent skills before installation, detecting 64 vulnerability patterns across 16 categories: prompt injection (5), data exfiltration (4), privilege escalation (3), supply chain (6), excessive agency (4), output handling (3), system prompt leakage (3), memory poisoning (3), tool misuse (3), rogue agent (2), trigger abuse (3), behavioral AST (8), taint tracking (5), YARA signatures (4), MCP least privilege (4), and MCP tool poisoning (4). Two-stage analysis: fast static pass then optional LLM semantic check. Live CVE lookups against OSV.dev. Multi-format output: terminal, JSON, Markdown, SARIF. Risk score 0–100. NVIDIA claims over 26% of common agent skills contain vulnerabilities. Python 97.3%; Apache-2.0; 5.3k stars.
key_takeaways: The MCP tool poisoning category (TP1–TP4) is new and specific to 2026's threat landscape: it detects hidden instructions in tool metadata (HTML comments, zero-width characters, base64 data URIs), Unicode deception (homoglyphs, RTL overrides), parameter description injection, and description-behavior mismatch via LLM. These are vectors that did not exist in traditional security scanners.

Behavioral AST analysis (8 patterns) catches exec(), eval(), dynamic imports, subprocess calls, and dangerous execution chains without needing to run the code — pure static analysis on the skill file structure. Taint tracking follows data flows from source (env vars, user input) to sink (network, exec) across variable assignments.

The SARIF output format means SkillSpector results can be imported directly into GitHub Advanced Security, Azure DevOps, or any SARIF-compatible security dashboard — enabling pre-installation skill scanning as a gate in a CI/CD pipeline.
top_picks.results: 5.3k GitHub stars; 23 commits; Apache-2.0. NVIDIA's stated figure: over 26% of common agent skills contain vulnerabilities. SARIF output enables integration with GitHub Advanced Security. Source: github.com/NVIDIA/SkillSpector (fetched June 13, 2026).
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Run SkillSpector as a pre-installation gate in your internal agent skill approval workflow. For any skill repo being evaluated: `skillspector scan <repo-url>`. For CI/CD integration, use `--format sarif` to emit a SARIF report and import into GitHub Advanced Security or your SAST pipeline. For internal skill registries, run SkillSpector on every new skill PR as a non-blocking gate initially, then graduate to blocking once false-positive rates are understood. The live OSV.dev CVE lookup (SC4) requires network access — for air-gapped environments, use `--offline` to disable live lookups and maintain a mirrored CVE database. | Regulated-environment caveats: SkillSpector's LLM semantic pass (if enabled) sends skill content to an LLM endpoint — route this to an internally approved model endpoint rather than the default. The static analysis pass is fully local and safe for regulated environments. YARA signature checks run locally against bundled signature packs; review the included YARA rules before fleet deployment. Pin the Python package version in your internal package registry. | 30-day experiment: Run SkillSpector on your currently installed agent skills library (all skills in your CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and Cursor rules files). Generate an HTML report. Classify each finding as actionable risk, acceptable risk, or false positive. Report the percentage of skills with at least one HIGH or CRITICAL finding. Use this baseline to define your internal skill approval policy.

top_picks.title: commensa-ai/commensa-audit
top_picks.subtitle: One-page rework report from git history — 27% of 162 agent-built PRs were AI self-correction, local-first, read-only, signal-cascade classification, MIT
top_picks.author: commensa-ai

secondary_urls.label: Show HN: I audited 162 agent-written PRs – 27% were the AI fixing itself

top_picks.summary: commensa-audit reads a GitHub repo's last 500 PRs and classifies each as generative or corrective using a transparent signal cascade: explicit corrective title/revert → self-correction (PR predominantly undoes lines from the prior N days) → churn-cluster membership → otherwise generative. Output: rework tax (share of PRs and changed lines correcting earlier work), superseded work (PRs whose output was entirely replaced), abandoned attempts (closed without merging), churn clusters (chains rewriting each other), line survival, hotspots by module, and agent-marked share. The authors' own 162-PR, 13-day sprint showed 27% rework tax. Read-only, local-first. Python 57.1%; MIT.
key_takeaways: A 27% rework tax on a 162-PR sprint means roughly 1 in 4 PRs is the agent correcting its own earlier output — this cost does not appear in token counts, API billing, or PR velocity metrics, but it does appear in git history. commensa-audit makes it visible for the first time.

The churn-cluster metric surfaces the worst failure mode: chains of PRs rewriting each other (e.g., 'it took 10 PRs to get dark mode right'). This pattern is invisible in standard engineering metrics but measurable from git history alone.

The agent-marked share is explicitly stated as a lower bound, never an attribution claim — absence of an agent marker (Co-Authored-By trailer, body signature) is not evidence of human authorship. This makes the tool conservative: it will not overstate AI contribution.
top_picks.results: The authors' own sprint: 162 PRs, 13 days, 27% rework tax. Tool covers newest 500 PRs by default. Output: HTML report (self-contained, forwardable), JSON export, per-PR CSV. Source: github.com/commensa-ai/commensa-audit (fetched June 13, 2026).
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Point commensa-audit at any GitHub repo your team is actively developing with agents: `python commensa_audit.py --repo <org>/<repo>`. The read-only, local-first design means no data leaves the developer machine and no write access to the repo is needed. Run monthly to track whether your quality gate investments (agent-skills, SkillSpector, /tdd) are reducing the rework tax. Use the hotspots output to identify which modules accumulate the most AI-generated churn — these are candidates for additional human review gates or more constrained agent scope. | Regulated-environment caveats: The tool reads GitHub API data via a personal access token; scope the token to `repo:read` only. For on-premises GitHub Enterprise, the GitHub API endpoint is configurable. The agent-marked share heuristic relies on Co-Authored-By trailers and PR body signatures — standardize these conventions across your team to improve signal quality. For squash-merge workflows, line survival metrics will be optimistic; note this in reporting. | 30-day experiment: Run commensa-audit on your primary AI-assisted development repo for the past 30 days. Calculate your baseline rework tax. Install one quality gate (addyosmani/agent-skills /review skill or a /tdd skill). Run commensa-audit again after 30 days. Report whether the rework tax moved.

top_picks.title: revfactory/harness
top_picks.subtitle: Meta-skill team-architecture factory for Claude Code — 6 agent team patterns, generates agent definitions + skills from one sentence, 6.6k stars, Apache-2.0
top_picks.author: revfactory

secondary_urls.label: Harness tutorial — Build an Entire AI Agent Team With Claude Code

top_picks.summary: harness is a meta-skill for Claude Code that designs multi-agent teams from a single sentence. It generates agent definitions (.claude/agents/) and skills (.claude/skills/) tailored to the domain using one of six pre-defined team-architecture patterns: Pipeline (sequential dependent tasks), Fan-out/Fan-in (parallel independent tasks), Expert Pool (context-dependent selective invocation), Producer-Reviewer (generation + quality review), Supervisor (central agent with dynamic task distribution), and Hierarchical Delegation (top-down recursive delegation). Trigger: 'build a harness for this project.' HTML 100%; Apache-2.0; 4.6k stars; +1,553 weekly delta.
key_takeaways: harness is a factory that builds other factories: it does not execute tasks; it generates the agent team architecture, role definitions, and skill assignments for a domain. The output is a versioned set of agent definitions and skills that can then be reviewed, modified, and committed like code.

The six team patterns are not arbitrary: Pipeline, Fan-out/Fan-in, Expert Pool, Producer-Reviewer, Supervisor, and Hierarchical Delegation map to the six canonical multi-agent coordination patterns described in agent framework documentation. An enterprise team can select the pattern appropriate to their workflow structure rather than inventing one from scratch.

The meta-skill concept means harness itself is a Claude Code skill — it is installed and invoked like any other skill, producing new skills and agent definitions as its output. This makes multi-agent system design reproducible and auditable: the harness invocation and its output both live in version control.
top_picks.results: +1,553 weekly star delta; 6,663 total stars (4.6k confirmed at fetch); 644 forks; 6 contributors; Apache-2.0. Source: github.com/revfactory/harness; youtube.com/watch?v=xFemCQdqy3Y (fetched June 13, 2026).
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: Implementation pattern: Install harness as a Claude Code plugin and invoke with 'build a harness for [domain description]'. Review the generated agent definitions and skills before committing — each generated agent definition specifies role, tools, scope, and escalation behavior. Use the Fan-out/Fan-in pattern for parallelizable research or analysis workflows; use Producer-Reviewer for code generation with mandatory human-equivalent review; use Supervisor for workflows where task prioritization changes dynamically. | Regulated-environment caveats: harness writes to .claude/agents/ and .claude/skills/ in the project directory — review generated agent definitions before fleet deployment, particularly tool access declarations and scope constraints. The generated agents inherit whatever model endpoint is configured for Claude Code — confirm generated agents are routed to your approved endpoint. For air-gapped environments, harness itself runs locally; the generated agents may call external APIs depending on the domain harness is applied to. | 30-day experiment: Identify one multi-step workflow your team currently runs manually or with ad-hoc agents (e.g., weekly repo audit, sprint retrospective prep, automated test generation for a new feature). Invoke harness to generate a team architecture for it. Review and adjust the generated agent definitions. Run the team for one sprint. Compare completion time and error rate against the manual or ad-hoc baseline.

items.summary: fleet's Show HN thread documents the only publicly verified three-tier agent cost architecture this week: (1) strong frontier model for task analysis/design and adding tasks to the queue; (2) local qwen3.6:36B on 2 GPUs (36GB total, 256K context, Ollama) as workers — slower but free; (3) strong frontier model again for validation and creating fix tasks. Git worktrees isolate workers per task. The beads task queue (Dolt-backed) handles dependencies, priorities, and multi-worker claiming. 3 workers running concurrently was found optimal — near 100% GPU utilization, questions answered overnight via Telegram.

items.title: The agent governance stack: addyosmani/agent-skills + SkillSpector + guard-skills + agent-gate
items.summary: Four independently deployable tools that compose into a complete agent governance pipeline this week: agent-skills enforces engineering-grade workflows during coding (pre-generation); SkillSpector scans skills before installation (pre-deployment); guard-skills catches lint failures, test gaps, and missing docs before code ships (pre-merge); agent-gate validates PRs for scope compliance, workflow permission escalation, and MCP config drift (pre-merge CI). The stack is fully local except agent-gate's GitHub API calls for PR data.

items.title: tastyeffectco/sandboxd — open-source engine for AI app-builder products with isolated agent sandboxes
items.summary: sandboxd documents the infrastructure pattern for AI app-builder products: isolated Linux containers, per-user filesystem and memory limits, built-in Claude Code and OpenCode agent support, live preview URLs, idle/wake lifecycle (saves memory, preserves files), Go control plane + Traefik routing + SQLite state. v0.1.1 (June 7, 2026). The architecture separates agent execution from preview serving — agents run in the sandboxd container; preview traffic routes through Traefik to the sandboxed app. Self-hosted on one Docker host, no Kubernetes.

sections.title: Automation Wins
sections.description: n8n, Make, and custom automations with measurable outcomes from the week of June 8–14, 2026.

items.title: n8n community template library passes 10,000 workflows — largest self-hostable AI automation library
items.summary: n8n's community-contributed workflow template library passed 10,000 automations on June 10, 2026. Announced on LinkedIn. Every template is community-built, fully inspectable, and deployable on private self-hosted infrastructure. Covers data transformation, API orchestration, AI agent workflows, database operations, and cross-platform integrations. New templates include an AI-powered KPI report template (revenue, ROAS, CAC, growth rates — delivered to email/Slack/WhatsApp/Telegram daily via cron) and a contract review workflow for legal compliance. n8n reached v2.25.7 this week with credential-picker data isolation fixes.
items.results: 10,000+ community-contributed templates as of June 10, 2026. Self-hostable; private infrastructure deployment supported. KPI template automates ROAS, CAC, revenue growth rate calculation and plain-language AI summary. Source: createwith.com/tool/n8n (fetched June 13, 2026).

items.title: LangGraph 1.2.4 per-node timeouts + DeltaChannel: long-running agents no longer silently stall or blow up checkpoint storage
items.summary: LangGraph 1.2.4 (early June 2026) adds per-node timeouts (pass timeout= directly to add_node), run-level limits (run_timeout and idle_timeout), cooperative shutdown via RunControl (stops after current superstep, saves resumable checkpoint), and a beta DeltaChannel that persists only per-step deltas rather than re-serializing full state. With snapshot_frequency, long-thread storage stays roughly flat instead of growing linearly. CLI 0.4.29 adds HTTPS dev server cert support. These features address the two most common long-running agent failures: stuck nodes and checkpoint storage inflation.
items.results: Per-node timeouts cap individual node execution. DeltaChannel keeps storage flat (full snapshot every K steps + incremental deltas). RunControl enables clean pause/resume without process kill. Source: mer.vin/2026/06/langgraph-1-2... ; YouTube walkthrough (fetched June 13, 2026).

items.title: superloglabs/superlog — open-source agentic observability, OTel ingestion, AI-driven incident grouping and self-healing
items.summary: Superlog ingests OTel traces, logs, and metrics, groups them into incidents using AI agents, and surfaces a self-healing agentic layer above standard observability tooling. TypeScript 97.6%; Apache-2.0; 820 stars. Architecture: web app + API + OTLP ingest proxy + worker processes (incident grouping, background jobs) + Postgres + ClickHouse + pluggable agent runner interfaces. Community edition fully open-source; hosted cloud tier with free tier and pay-as-you-go. Created June 2, 2026.
items.results: 820 stars; 124 commits; Apache-2.0; launched June 2, 2026. Community edition fully open-source. Source: github.com/superloglabs/superlog (fetched June 13, 2026).

sections.title: Framework Releases
sections.description: Meaningful framework releases from the week of June 8–14, 2026 — major versions or new capabilities only.

items.title: LangGraph 1.2.4 — per-node timeouts, DeltaChannel, RunControl, CLI 0.4.29 HTTPS (June 2–11, 2026)
items.summary: LangGraph 1.2.4 lands four significant changes: (1) per-node timeout= parameter on add_node with configurable timeout_policy; (2) run_timeout and idle_timeout run-level limits — idle_timeout resets on every progress step, catching silently stuck agents; (3) RunControl cooperative shutdown after current superstep, saving a resumable checkpoint; (4) beta DeltaChannel that persists only deltas with periodic full snapshots, keeping long-thread storage flat. CLI 0.4.28 adds ty type checker and TS 6 tooling; CLI 0.4.29 adds HTTPS dev server cert support. Production classifier; post-v1.0.

items.title: n8n 2.26.0 — AI workflow grounding, MCP OAuth token fix, sub-agent tool call resolution (June 2026)
items.summary: n8n 2.26.0 ships: ground AI workflow completion in saved graph (agent workflows tied to committed state); fix hardcoded `aud` claim in MCP OAuth tokens (unblocking MCP-authenticated workflows); resolve sub-agent tool calls inline when nested (LangChain agent node); prefer MCP registry nodes when wiring AI Agent tools; move instance AI builds to a skill; sub-workflows respect own timeout settings. 2.25.7 also released (credential-picker data isolation to workflow-level context). Two releases in the week; both targeted at production AI workflow reliability.

items.title: CrewAI — 52k+ stars, native MCP and A2A protocol support, Flows event-driven architecture
items.summary: CrewAI reached 52,000 GitHub stars as of this week. Recent additions: native MCP and A2A protocol support (per Morph AI framework comparison); Flows feature (event-driven @start, @listen, @router decorators for deterministic branching across multiple crews); unified LanceDB memory backend with LLM-analyzed fact extraction, hierarchical scope tree, and 0.85 similarity threshold deduplication; 30+ built-in tools. Fastest path to a working multi-agent prototype. Practical pattern: CrewAI to prototype, LangGraph to productionize when state rigor is non-negotiable.

sections.title: Emerging Patterns
sections.description: Cross-source patterns observed across repos and discussions for the week of June 8–14, 2026.

items.title: Agent skills now need the same governance stack as code dependencies: versioning, security scanning, and quality gates
items.summary: Four independent signals converged this week: addyosmani/agent-skills (engineering lifecycle), mattpocock/skills (3.20x eval improvement with structured skills), NVIDIA/SkillSpector (64-pattern security scanner before install), and amElnagdy/guard-skills (fail-safe quality gates before merge). The pattern is now deployable end-to-end: define skills with engineering practices → scan skills for vulnerabilities before installation → gate agent output against quality thresholds before merge → audit rework tax post-sprint (commensa-audit). This is not a roadmap; all four tools exist and work today.

items.title: Production agent pipelines are converging on a three-tier model cost architecture: frontier model for design, local model for execution, frontier model for validation
items.summary: Two independent signals this week validated the same architecture. sermakarevich/fleet (Show HN, June 14): strong frontier model for task analysis and queue management, qwen3.6:36B on local GPU for parallel workers, strong model for validation and fix-task creation. The AI agent DN42 incident (HN, June 12): unconstrained frontier model given cloud credentials with no spend limits burned $6,531 in 24 hours — the opposite of this pattern. The three-tier approach decouples reasoning cost from execution cost and keeps production-scale parallelism affordable.

items.title: Meta-skills that design agent teams before execution are emerging as a distinct category above individual skill libraries
items.summary: revfactory/harness (meta-skill that generates agent teams and skill sets) and the parallel emergence of phuryn/pm-skills (65-skill PM lifecycle) and addyosmani/agent-skills (7-command engineering lifecycle) represent three levels of the same architecture: individual skills (mattpocock/skills), domain-specific skill libraries (pm-skills, agent-skills), and meta-skills that generate teams and skills for arbitrary domains (harness). The meta-skill layer is now deployable and open-source. An enterprise team can invoke harness to generate a purpose-built agent team for any internal workflow without designing the team architecture from scratch.
